743.title: Let them come
743.hook: Jews sit shiva; some Muslim families receive mourners for three days: grief is meant to be accompanied
743.howItsDone: Jewish mourners sit shiva at home while the community visits and brings food, and in some Muslim families relatives and neighbors receive visitors and send meals for three days after a death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hand on the heart. Your line was this is hard. Did you say it once to yourself, plainly, the way you'd say it to a friend? A new week starts now. Day seven hundred forty-three.

A casserole dish on a doorstep, covered in foil, with a note taped to the lid. By evening there's another. Then a bag of bagels, a tray of fruit, somebody's aunt at the door with a pot of soup. On some streets, when there's been a death, the food starts arriving before anyone asks for it. And for the family inside, the hard part may not be cooking at all. It's opening the door. Yesterday turned care inward. Today turns it around again. In more than one tradition, grief is not meant to be carried alone in a quiet house. It is meant to have company.
screen: `A DISH ON THE DOORSTEP.` → `THE HARD PART: OPENING THE DOOR.` → `GRIEF IS MEANT TO HAVE COMPANY.`

segments.voice: First, the seven days. In Jewish tradition, after a burial, the close family sits shiva. They stay home, and the community comes to them. The Bible already knows a seven-day mourning: when Jacob dies, Genesis says of his son Joseph, "he made a mourning for his father seven days." Some families leave the front door unlocked during shiva, so visitors can let themselves in and the mourners don't have to get up. Second, the first meal. Jewish tradition, recorded in the Talmud, says the first meal after the burial should come from someone else's hands, not the mourner's own kitchen. Neighbors cook. The mourner's job is to eat. Third, the same instinct in another house. A hadith tells of the day news came that a man named Ja'far had died. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, told the people to prepare food for Ja'far's family, because something had come to them that would keep them busy. It's in the collections of Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi. In some Muslim families today, relatives and neighbors receive visitors and bring meals for three days. Fourth, the other side of the door. Every one of these customs needs two people. Someone carries the soup up the path. Someone else has to open the door and take it. For a person who is used to being the helper, that second job can feel like the harder one. In these traditions, saying yes to the casserole isn't a failure at grieving. It is part of how grieving is done. The visitors come. The mourner lets them.
screen: `SEVEN DAYS AT HOME.` · `THE FIRST MEAL FROM OTHER HANDS.` · `FOOD FOR JA'FAR'S FAMILY.` · `SOMEONE HAS TO OPEN THE DOOR.` · then, large: `LET THEM COME.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one person who has offered help, recently or a while ago, help you waved away. Or someone who would come if you asked. You don't have to call them now. Just let the door open in your mind, and let them stand there with whatever they're carrying. Notice what happens when you imagine saying yes. If something tightens, breathe there. If you pray, you can bring that person to God by name. Then, for the rest of the sit, simply breathe, as someone who is allowed to be cared for. The bell holds the time.
Let them come. From shiva to the meals sent to Ja'far's family, mourning customs meet grief with company, and the mourner's part is to let it in. Today's word.
Your line: let them come. Today, say yes to one offer of help, however small: a ride, a coffee, a hand with the bags. Day seven hundred forty-three.

744.title: One small mercy
744.hook: on a bad day, look for one small mercy
744.howItsDone: Jewish and Christian readers return to Lamentations 3:22–23, 'they are new every morning', on hard days, and some people keep a nightly habit of naming one good thing from the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a dish on the doorstep. Your line was let them come. Did you say yes to one offer of help, even a small one? Day seven hundred forty-four.

The alarm didn't go off. The train sat in a tunnel, going nowhere. There was a hard email before lunch, and a call from the clinic that ended with, we'll need to run more tests. Then, on the walk home, a stranger held the door at the corner shop, and there was one of the good rolls left, still warm. Small. Nearly nothing. It didn't fix the day. But it was there. An old book of grief has a line about exactly that kind of thing, set right in the middle of its sorrow.
screen: `A DAY GOING WRONG.` → `ONE WARM ROLL.` → `A LINE IN A BOOK OF GRIEF.`

segments.voice: First, where the line lives. Lamentations is a book of poems over a ruined city. It is full of anguish. In the third chapter the poet says, "thou hast removed my soul far off from peace: I forgat prosperity." He has forgotten what good even feels like. Second, the turn. A few verses later, nothing outside has changed. The city is still in ruins. But he writes, "This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope." And then: "It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning." Notice the verb. He recalls. He doesn't deny the ruins; he turns his attention, on purpose, to something else that is also true. Third, the word. The Hebrew behind mercies is hesed. English Bibles translate it in different ways: mercy, kindness, lovingkindness. Jews and Christians read these lines as being about God's faithfulness. Someone with no faith in God can still borrow the move underneath: recall one thing that was kind today. Fourth, why small. This is not a silver lining. Last week, the line was growth isn't required, and that still stands. A small mercy doesn't explain the bad day or make it worth it. It doesn't cancel the test results. It just sits next to them: a warm roll, a held door, a text from a friend. The poet in Lamentations doesn't stop lamenting after this verse. The book goes on grieving. He has simply found one thing to hold while it does.
screen: `A BOOK OF POEMS OVER RUINS.` · `THIS I RECALL TO MY MIND.` · `HESED: MERCY, KINDNESS.` · `NOT A SILVER LINING.` · then, large: `ONE SMALL MERCY.`

segments.voice: Settle. Let today, or yesterday if today has barely started, play back for a moment, hard parts included. Don't argue with them. Then look for one small mercy in it. Small enough to miss: a kind word, hot water, a song in a shop, a minute when nothing hurt. When you find it, stay with it. Name it once, quietly. If you pray, you can give thanks for it in your own words, or with the line from Lamentations: they are new every morning. Then breathe beside it until the bell. The bell holds the time.
One small mercy. From Lamentations: in the middle of ruin, the poet recalls mercies that are new every morning. Not a fix. One thing to hold. Today's word.
Your line: one small mercy. Tonight, before sleep, find one from today, however tiny, and name it. Day seven hundred forty-four.

745.title: The wounded healer
745.hook: people who have suffered sometimes become healers, an old idea found in myths and in modern care alike
745.howItsDone: Some recovery groups and peer support programs pair people who have come through an illness, addiction or loss with those newly facing it, and some Christians read 2 Corinthians 1:4 as a call to pass on the comfort they have received.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a warm roll on a bad day. Your line was one small mercy. Did you find one before sleep? Day seven hundred forty-five.

In Greek myth there's a centaur named Chiron, half man, half horse, who lives in a cave on a mountain and teaches young heroes. He knows herbs, music and medicine. In some tellings he teaches healing to Asclepius, who becomes the god of medicine. And Chiron carries a wound of his own: an arrow, poisoned, that struck him by accident. He is immortal, so he cannot die of it. And it will not heal. The one who teaches healing cannot heal himself. That strange picture has followed people a long way, into churches and clinics. It has a name.
screen: `A CENTAUR WHO TEACHES HEALING.` → `A WOUND THAT WON'T CLOSE.` → `IT HAS A NAME.`

segments.voice: First, the myth. Chiron's wound doesn't stop his work. In the story, it sits right beside it. Much later, the psychiatrist Carl Jung wrote of the wounded physician: the idea that a healer's own hurt can be part of what lets them understand a patient's. Writers after him tied that phrase to Chiron. Second, the letter. Paul, writing to the church at Corinth, puts the same idea in Christian terms. He calls God the one "who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God." Comfort received becomes comfort passed on. The Catholic priest Henri Nouwen wrote a whole book called The Wounded Healer, about how a minister's own loneliness and pain can become a place where others find welcome. Third, the room down the hall. The idea isn't only old. Some recovery groups are built on it: a person who has been through it, sitting with a person going through it. Some hospitals and clinics bring in peer supporters, people with lived experience of an illness, to sit beside those newly facing it. Nobody has to explain what the first night feels like. Fourth, a caution. Nobody owes their wound to anyone, and some wounds are still too open to lend out. One way to put it: help from a scar, not from a fresh cut. On some days, you are the one who needs the soup. On others, what you came through may be what someone else needs to hear.
screen: `CHIRON: THE HEALER WHO HURTS.` · `COMFORT RECEIVED, COMFORT PASSED ON.` · `SOMEONE WHO HAS BEEN THROUGH IT.` · `FROM A SCAR, NOT A FRESH CUT.` · then, large: `THE WOUND HELPS.`

segments.voice: Settle. Let one hard thing you've come through come to mind, one that has begun to heal, not one still raw. Ask quietly: what did I learn in there that someone else might need? A phone number. A sentence that helped. Something nobody told you at the start. Then let one person come to mind who is near the beginning of something like it. You don't need to reach out now. Just hold them, and what you might offer. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.

The wounded healer. From Chiron in Greek myth, through Paul's comfort passed on, to people with lived experience sitting with the newly hurt: what you came through can help someone else. Today's word.
Your line: the wound helps. Today, if the moment is right, offer one person something you learned the hard way, gently, without a lecture. Day seven hundred forty-five.

746.title: Not punishment
746.hook: Job's friends were wrong: suffering isn't proof you've failed
746.howItsDone: Jewish and Christian readers turn to the book of Job, Luke 13:1–5 and Ecclesiastes 9:11 when someone asks whether a disaster was deserved, and some pastoral counselors use these texts to gently challenge the idea that suffering is proof of guilt.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chiron and his wound. Your line was the wound helps. Did you pass on one thing you learned the hard way? Day seven hundred forty-six.

Some people arrive with terrible news. Pilate has killed a group of Galileans, men from up north, while they were offering their sacrifices. Their blood is mixed with the blood of the animals. In Luke's Gospel, the people tell this to Jesus, and there's a question hanging in the air that nobody says out loud. Then he says it for them: "Suppose ye that these Galilaeans were sinners above all the Galilaeans, because they suffered such things?" It's an old question, and it doesn't only come up in Luke. It comes up after a diagnosis, a layoff, a crash. What did they do to deserve it? What did I?
screen: `TERRIBLE NEWS FROM GALILEE.` → `THE QUESTION NOBODY SAYS.` → `WHAT DID I DO?`

segments.voice: First, the old equation. Suffer, and you must have done something. It's the logic of Job's friends. Eliphaz asks Job to name one innocent person who ever perished, as if the answer settled things. At the end of the book, God tells the friends they have not spoken rightly, as Job has. The book of Job doesn't explain suffering. But it does refuse the equation. Second, the answer in Luke. Jesus answers his own question: "I tell you, Nay." Then he raises a second disaster, one with no villain at all: "those eighteen, upon whom the tower in Siloam fell, and slew them, think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem?" And again: "I tell you, Nay." Third, the hard line after it. Jesus goes on: "except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish." Readers take that in different ways. Some hear it as a call to everyone listening to turn to God, because life is short and nobody is safe. Others hear a warning about the coming troubles of that time. What it doesn't do is say the eighteen earned the tower. Fourth, time and chance. Ecclesiastes, a book of the Hebrew Bible, puts it plainly: "time and chance happeneth to them all." Towers fall. Cells divide wrong. Companies close. Some suffering has causes we can name and change, and that's worth knowing. But in these texts, a hard thing landing on someone is not, by itself, a verdict on that someone. That holds for the people on the news, and it holds closer to home.
screen: `THE OLD EQUATION.` · `I TELL YOU, NAY.` · `THE HARD LINE AFTER IT.` · `TIME AND CHANCE.` · then, large: `NOT PUNISHMENT.`

segments.voice: Settle. Is there something hard in your life that you've quietly filed under my fault, or what I deserve? Not a real mistake you might want to make right. A story that says the suffering itself proves something bad about you. Hold it lightly for a moment. Then, on an out-breath, set it down, the way you'd set down a heavy bag at the door. You can pick it up again later if you choose. For now, just breathe without it. If you pray, you can hand it to God. The bell holds the time.

Not punishment. From Job's friends, who were told they hadn't spoken rightly, to the tower of Siloam and the answer, I tell you, nay: suffering is not, by itself, proof that someone failed. Today's word.
Your line: not punishment. Today, if you catch yourself or anyone asking what they did to deserve it, answer quietly: not punishment. Day seven hundred forty-six.

747.title: Not numb
747.hook: how to hold the world's suffering, war and hunger, without going numb
747.howItsDone: Some people keep a small, regular gift for one distant cause, so hard news has somewhere to go; others hold a named place in prayer, or write to someone in a position to help.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Job's friends got it wrong: pain is not proof of failure. Your line was not punishment. Did one shaming story loosen its grip? Today, pain that belongs to strangers far away. Day seven hundred forty-seven.

Eleven at night. A phone lights up on the nightstand. A headline about a war. Under it, a photo of a line of people waiting for bread. A thumb hovers for a second. Then it keeps moving: a recipe, a joke, a friend's new haircut. Nobody in that moment is cruel. The heart has simply been asked to hold more than one heart can hold, and it closes the door a little. That closing has a name in everyday speech: going numb. Today, two old voices on how to keep the door open without being flattened by what comes through.
screen: `A HEADLINE AT ELEVEN AT NIGHT.` → `THE THUMB KEEPS MOVING.` → `THE DOOR CLOSES A LITTLE.`

segments.voice: First, the Chinese teacher Mencius. In one passage he asks his listeners to imagine a person who suddenly sees a small child about to fall into a well. Anyone, he says, would feel a jolt of alarm and pity. Not to win the parents' favor, not to be praised, not because the child's crying is annoying. Just that jolt. Mencius calls that feeling a beginning of kindness, and some readers picture it as a sprout, the first shoot of a plant. A sprout is small, and it can be trampled. It can also be tended. Second, what numbness is. Read with Mencius in mind, it isn't proof that someone has no heart. It can be a sprout that got too much weather at once. The feeling doesn't die; it goes under, because it had nowhere to go. Third, a voice from Jewish tradition. In the Mishnah, in the collection called the Sayings of the Fathers, Rabbi Tarfon says something like this: the work is not yours to finish, and you are not free to walk away from it. Two halves, both needed. The first half lifts the weight: no one person ends a war or a famine. The second half keeps the door open: walking away entirely isn't the answer either. Fourth, put the two together, each in its own place. Mencius says the feeling is a beginning. Tarfon says do your part without needing to complete the whole. The feeling stays alive when it is given one small thing to do. A gift, a letter, learning a place's name and where it is on the map. Not everything. One thing.
screen: `A CHILD AT THE EDGE OF A WELL.` · `NUMB IS A SPROUT UNDER TOO MUCH WEATHER.` · `NOT YOURS TO FINISH, NOT FREE TO LEAVE.` · `GIVE THE FEELING ONE THING TO DO.` · then, large: `NOT NUMB.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one place in the world where people are suffering now. Just one. Say its name quietly. Notice whatever comes: a jolt, a tiredness, nothing much at all. Any of it is fine. Then, without leaving the breath, choose one act for that place. A small gift. A message to someone who can help. Reading one honest account from there. If you pray, you can hold that place in prayer. Decide when you'll do it today. The bell holds the time.
Not numb: keeping the heart's first jolt alive by giving it one small thing to do, without needing to finish the whole work. Today's word.
Your line: not numb. Today, give or act once for a pain far from you, and let that one act be enough for today. Day seven hundred forty-seven.

screen: `DAY 747 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ONE DAY AT A TIME.`

748.title: One day at a time
748.hook: Jesus: sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof (Matthew 6:34)
748.howItsDone: Some Christians pray the Lord's Prayer each morning, asking for 'this day our daily bread', and turn to Matthew 6 in anxious seasons; recovery groups use the phrase 'one day at a time' in a similar spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a child at the edge of a well, and a saying about work you don't have to finish. Your line was not numb. What one thing did you do for a far-off place? Day seven hundred forty-eight.

"Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof." It sounds like something carved over a door in an old courthouse. It is actually the last line of a short talk about worry, in the Gospel of Matthew, and in the story Jesus says it to a crowd on a hillside. The text calls them the multitudes: people with bills, harvests and children of their own to worry about. He doesn't tell them their troubles are imaginary. He tells them something stranger. Today has enough of its own.
screen: `A LINE THAT SOUNDS LIKE A COURTHOUSE.` → `A CROWD ON A HILLSIDE.` → `TODAY HAS ENOUGH OF ITS OWN.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. In the King James Bible the passage keeps saying "take no thought." Readers sometimes hear that as don't plan. The talk is about worry, the kind that runs ahead and chews on things that haven't happened. Second, the birds and the flowers. "Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them." And then: "Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin." In between, a question with a smile in it: "Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature?" Worry, it turns out, doesn't make anyone taller. Third, the closing line in full. "Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof." Evil here means trouble, hardship. Notice what the line admits. Today has trouble. It doesn't promise an easy day. It says one day's share is enough to carry, and tomorrow's share can wait for tomorrow. Fourth, where it sits. The same sermon, a little earlier, holds the prayer Christians call the Lord's Prayer, with its line "Give us this day our daily bread." Bread for this day. Not a year's supply. Some readers hear the two together: trust practiced one day at a time. And the same shape turns up outside the church too, in recovery rooms and hospital waiting rooms: handle today. Just today.
screen: `TAKE NO THOUGHT: A TALK ABOUT WORRY.` · `BIRDS, LILIES, AND ONE CUBIT.` · `SUFFICIENT UNTO THE DAY.` · `BREAD FOR THIS DAY.` · then, large: `TODAY IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the shoulders drop. Bring up whatever is weighing on you. Now sort it, gently. What belongs to today: a call, a meal, a page, one conversation. And what belongs to a later day: the test next month, the bill next season, the thing that might happen. Picture setting the later things on a shelf. They'll be there. You can pick them up on their own day. For now, hold only today's share, and breathe with it. If you pray, you can ask for today's bread and nothing more. The bell holds the time.
One day at a time: carrying only today's share, because, in Matthew's words, sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof. Today's word.
screen: `ONE DAY AT A TIME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: today is enough. When a worry about next week arrives today, ask whose day it belongs to, and put it back on the shelf. Day seven hundred forty-eight.

fork.reveal: "the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself." it doesn't deny the trouble; it gives each day its own share.

749.title: Tisha B'Av
749.hook: on the ninth of Av, Jews mourn the destruction of the Temples and read Lamentations
749.howItsDone: On Tisha B'Av, observant Jews fast, sit low as mourners do, and hear Lamentations (Eikhah) chanted in the synagogue; the plea 'renew our days as of old' is repeated at the end of the reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, birds, lilies and the line sufficient unto the day. Your line was today is enough. A week's end, too: mourners let in, one small mercy, the wounded healer, not punishment, not numb, today is enough. Now, days set aside for mourning. Day seven hundred forty-nine.
screen: `TODAY IS ENOUGH.` · `A WEEK OF PRACTICES FOR HARD DAYS.`

segments.voice: A summer evening. In a synagogue the lights are low. Some people are sitting on the floor or on low stools, the way mourners sit at a shiva. Nobody greets each other with the usual warmth. Someone begins to read from a short book of poems, in a slow, falling chant. The first word is a cry: how. On this one day of the year, a whole community sits like a family at a funeral, for a loss that happened long before anyone in the room was born. The day is called Tisha B'Av.
screen: `LIGHTS LOW, PEOPLE ON THE FLOOR.` → `A SLOW, FALLING CHANT.` → `A FUNERAL FOR A CITY.`

segments.voice: First, the date. Tisha B'Av names a day on the Jewish calendar, the ninth of the month of Av. The Mishnah, the early collection of Jewish teaching, lists the calamities tradition remembers on that day, among them the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem, the first time and the second. It is kept as a fast. Second, the book. The reading is Lamentations, short poems of grief for Jerusalem. A few days ago we heard a turn in its third chapter; this reading starts at the very beginning. Its Hebrew name is its first word, Eikhah: how. In the King James Bible it opens, "How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow!" Your line today says it in plain modern words: how lonely sits the city. Third, the picture. The poet doesn't describe rubble. The city becomes a woman sitting alone, a widow, weeping in the night with no one to comfort her. Grief that is too big for a list of facts gets a body and a face. That may be why the book still works: a person can sit beside a person. Fourth, the ending. The last chapter turns to a plea: "Turn thou us unto thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned; renew our days as of old." Then one more verse, bitter, about being rejected. In the synagogue, the custom is to repeat the plea for renewal after it, so the reading does not end in the dark. Nothing is fixed. Nobody pretends the loss didn't happen. But the community grieves out loud, together, on a set day, and then rises from the floor.
screen: `THE NINTH OF AV, A DAY OF FASTING.` · `EIKHAH: HOW.` · `THE CITY AS A WIDOW.` · `RENEW OUR DAYS AS OF OLD.` · then, large: `HOW LONELY SITS THE CITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse. "How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow!" Read it once more, slowly, aloud or under your breath. Then sit with it. Let it stand for whatever it stands for today: a place you lost, a home that changed, a loss people around you carry. Or simply honor that a people has read these words in grief for a very long time. No need to fix anything. Sit beside it. The bell holds the time.
Tisha B'Av: the ninth of Av, the Jewish day of mourning for the Temples, when Lamentations is read low and slow. Today's word.
Your line: how lonely sits the city. Today, read one verse of Lamentations, and let grief have a set place instead of everywhere. Day seven hundred forty-nine.
